t: Michael Graves on Objects He Designs for Target, and Himself: Q&A - The New York Times
s: February 5, 2013 - They asked me to lunch and said, “We’ve been knocking you off for 20 years,” and said, “Maybe you’d like to come and try designing for us, if we can keep the price at a Target range.” So we designed half a dozen things for them, and they liked it so much they said, “Well, let’s keep going.” ... Just the opposite. It was my hope to do that. I had been designing for Alessi and Swid Powell and Steuben and high-end people, and people always complained, “Michael, we’d love to buy your stuff, but it’s too expensive.” I always wanted to do what Josef Hoffmann, Wiener Werkstätte and the Bauhaus wanted to do, which they never got to do because they designed in a craft mode.

t: Michael Graves's Work for Target: His Most Enduring Legacy? - Metropolis
s: August 11, 2021 - It was one thing when Graves created his teakettle for Alessi, in 1985, a witty if not entirely practical object that, despite its cost—it sells for about $100—became a kind of artifact of yuppiedom. It was quite another when Graves began designing objects for Target, the mass-market discount store where you could outfit an entire kitchen for $100.
